name: Poisson Regression
analogy: Think of it as forecasting how many customers walk through a shop door in the next five minutes. It first works out the typical arrival rate for current conditions, such as a busy lunch hour, then treats the actual count as a random draw around that rate. Busier conditions raise the rate by multiplying, never by going below zero.

steps.title: Take a target that counts events
steps.description: The target is a whole number of events in a bar: zero, one, two and so on. It can never be negative. The model learns what conditions make more events likely.
steps.inExample: The target is the number of trades of 20 contracts or more in each 5-minute MNQ bar, over 20,000 past bars.

steps.title: Combine the features into a score
steps.description: Each feature gets a weight, and the weighted features are added into one score. The score sits on a logarithmic scale, so that each feature raises or lowers the expected count by a percentage, not by a fixed amount.
steps.inExample: A high volume and a busy last bar push the score up, while being late in the session pulls it down.

steps.title: Exponentiate the score into an expected count
steps.description: The score is exponentiated, which always gives a positive number, so the expected count can never fall below zero. A weight reads as a rate ratio: each extra unit of a feature multiplies the expected count by a fixed factor.
steps.inExample: The bar's score becomes an expected count of 4 large trades in the next bar.

steps.title: Assume the spread equals the average
steps.description: The model assumes that the counts scatter around the average by an amount tied exactly to the average: a bar expecting 4 events typically deviates by about the square root of that. This is the model's key assumption and also its most common weak point.
steps.inExample: With an average of 4, the typical deviation from it is about 2 trades.

steps.title: Fit the weights to make the real counts likely
steps.description: Training adjusts the weights, using a repeated reweighted fitting routine, until the observed counts are as likely as possible under the model. If bars have different lengths, a fixed exposure term corrects for that without using up a weight.
steps.inExample: After 6 rounds on 20,000 bars the weights settle, with each doubling of relative volume raising the expected count by about a quarter.

steps.title: Check the spread against the assumption
steps.description: The fitted model's leftover scatter is compared with what the equal-spread assumption predicts. If real counts are far wilder than that, the model is too sure of itself, and a variant that allows extra spread is needed.
steps.inExample: The leftover scatter is about 40 percent larger than the assumption implies, a mild warning that the probabilities in the tails are slightly too tight.

useFor.example: Predicting how many large trades will print in the next 5-minute MNQ bar, to plan how aggressively an order can be worked.
Forecasting the number of price ticks in the next bar as a gauge of how fast the market will be moving.
Estimating how many block or iceberg orders per bar will appear, from order-flow features.
Estimating expected counts of large trades in the five minutes after an inflation report from past releases.

avoidWhen: Counts are much more spread out than their average, which is common in bursts; a negative binomial model allows that extra spread honestly.
Most bars have no events at all for a structural reason, such as no large participant being active; a zero-inflated model separates that from a low rate.

example.scenario: At 10:35 on an MNQ 5-minute chart, a trader wants to know how many trades of 20 or more contracts will print in the next bar, to judge how much block liquidity is likely to be around.

input.summary: Features for the bar that just closed, in the same form the model was trained on.

fields.name: large trades in the last bar
fields.meaning: How many trades of 20 contracts or more printed in the bar that just closed.

fields.name: volume against its 20-bar average
fields.meaning: How heavy trading was compared with the recent norm.

fields.name: average true range, 14 bars
fields.meaning: The typical high-to-low travel of a recent bar.

fields.name: minutes since the 09:30 open
fields.meaning: How far into the session the bar is.

fields.name: bar length
fields.meaning: The fixed exposure: every bar covers the same amount of time.

output.summary: An expected count and the chances of a few notable counts.

fields.name: expected number of large trades
fields.meaning: The score exponentiated: the model's average expectation for the next bar.

fields.name: chance of no large trades
fields.meaning: The probability that the next bar prints none.

fields.name: chance of 7 or more large trades
fields.meaning: The probability that the next bar is unusually busy.

example.reading: Expect around four large prints in the next bar, so a 20-contract order has company. The tail chances are narrower than reality if counts are bursty, so widen the 11 percent figure a little. Check on later bars whether the realized counts scatter as the model assumes.
